div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: —An old Hall in the Castle of De Mallory, decorated with Armour, Trophies, &c.

sp.p: Mercy on me, a second dismal day! and here am I likely to waste the precious hours of my youth, for a whole month. I shall begin to notch like Robinson Crusoe. My master, I hear, has some distant chance of inheriting this piece of melancholy magnificence; but it would be to him in every sense a dismal acquisition; for the best gentleman's gentleman in existence would then most peremptorily take his leave of him.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Ah, Mr. Spruce—here you are, I see— no doubt meditating and reflecting on departed heroes.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Yes, Sir, yes—and heartily wishing myself a departed hero too.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: That is nobly spoken.—Who would not die to obtain their renown?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Not I, upon my soul? for if I could not depart without dying, I'd stay here for ever, dull as it is.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Dull, Sir! I am heartily sorry we make De Mallory Castle so unpleasant to you.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: My dear friend, you mistake me. Your cheerful face is the only thing that comforts me— you look like a fine smiling evergreen in a church-yard, or like the comical gravedigger in Hamlet— full of merriment, though surrounded by the fragments of mortality.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Ha! you are a joker. But how does your worthy master, Sir Harry Aspen? I was not in the way when he arrived yesterday.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: My master is as usual, Sir, always on the fidget—but a servant, you know, should not expose his master's foibles.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Surely not, surely not.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Oh, I would not for kingdoms, tell any body what an absurd fellow my master is.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: If he be absurd, it would certainly be wrong in you to make it known.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Wrong! it would be criminal, Sir,—criminal in the last degree—and what of all things would most torment him; for the terror of his life, Sir, is being an object for people to laugh at!

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Be careful then.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: You need not caution me—particularly in this house; for, of all families in the world he would most dread being ridiculed here.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Certainly—a man can least bear disrespect from his own relations—he is, you know, a branch of the male line of this family.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Yes; and he is desirous to entwine with a branch of the female line of this family.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: ‘How do you mean?’

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: ‘He wants to blend branches’ with Lady ulia Sandford.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Poh, poh—you are jesting—Lady Julia is destined to be united to her cousin, Lord De Mallory, whom we are daily expecting.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Indeed! Don't be too sure of that.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: You are ignorant of the family arrangements, I find—well, well, I will enlighten you. You must know, then, that the present Lord De Mallory's grandfather, proud of his rank, and great alliances, and highly incensed at the marriage of one of his sisters in a way which he thought degrading, determined to take on himself the disposal of his family, down to the second generation.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: That was very considerate, and certainly the plan to save wavering dispositions a great deal of trouble. ‘How kind in one's grandfather to free one from the perplexity of thinking for one's self.’

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Well—his son, and his two daughters, he matched to his mind, during his life, and beheld them blessed with children;—this pleased him highly; for he now saw the prospect of excluding exceptionable alliances by intermarriages in his own illustrious house.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: This scheme must have comforted old Stately, marvellously.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Old Stately! Fie, fie—be more respectful.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: ‘Well, I'll try. Get on with your story. Heaven knows where it will end—we have already been through two generations.’

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: ‘Patience, you prattler!’ He entailed his immense estates on his grandson, the present Lord De Mallory, with the stipulation, that at a stated period, which is nearly arrived, he should marry his first cousin, Lady Julia Sandford.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: But how if she refuse?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Refuse! Impossible. Why, by refusing, she would forfeit every shilling of her fortune.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: My master doesn't care for that.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Plague take your master!

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: With all my heart.—But I say—suppose Lady Julia were to refuse Lord De Mallory, what is he to do then?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: He? Why then he must marry his other first cousin, the Honourable Miss Alford, who is now on a visit here.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: And if Lord De Mallory should be rebellious enough to oppose the intentions of his old match-making grandfather, and take a wife of his own choice, what would be the consequence to him?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Ruin. The whole family estate would go to your master, who, though a distant relation to Lord De Mallory, is the nearest male representative.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: What the devil is the alarm bell ringing for?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! The alarm bell! It is the bell in your master's chamber—it is only to alarm you.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Heaven preserve me! Between the sight of metal,
and the sound of it, my nerves will be shaking the whole time I am here.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: I see Lady Julia coming this way. Do go to Sir Harry, pray—be so kind as to leave me now, Mr. Spruce, or you will deprive me of the happiness of hearing her sweet tongue prattle— Bless her! she is an angel.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Yes; and I know who will be master of the angel. Well, with two such treasures,— an angel for a wife, and your humble servant for a valet, if he don't consider himself well appointed, he is a most unconscionable man.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Ah! dear Lady Julia—always cheerful, always gay—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Yes: it is good for the constitution— I intend to be a healthy blooming old gentlewoman. Only think, now, of your plump rosy cheeks at seventy-five—Why, you surely don't suppose that you owe those to nothing but air and exercise—Bless your merry old heart! if that had not beat to the tune of good-humour you would now have just such a wrinkled wizened phiz, as my Lady Fidget—and she is but forty-seven.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: You dear pleasant creature!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Besides, the pains it must take some people to make themselves miserable, who have not a trouble in the world, would not suit my indolent habits. Why there is Mrs. Carecourt with every comfort in life, but a husband—and she is rich enough to buy a dozen of the best that can be brought to market, yet will she, poor silly soul! lie awake a whole night, to hammer out vexations that may keep her awake for a fortnight to come.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Ah! my dear Lady, all are not blessed with your sweet disposition.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Why, then, let those who are not gifted, only labour half as hard to be happy, as they do to be wretched, and, my life for it, they succeed. It is very foolish that people don't know what they would be at—To be sure, they'll tell you, in an instant, what it is they most wish; but then they set about gaining their point, mighty oddly—One, is all for comfort; and is as cross as the very devil, that every body around, may contribute to give it her.—With another, oh! gaiety is the delight of her heart—and she therefore chooses to be dull and peevish, to encourage you to enliven her. Why won't the foolish creatures learn, that whatever is to be purchased, good humour is the coin to procure it?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Your sweet example would make the most froward, good tempered. Ah! Lady Julia, if Lord De Mallory should happen to have any little remains of his boyish ill-humours, how soon will your cheerfulness cure him!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I cure him! Impossible. No, no. I am not so daring a Doctor as to undertake such an obstinate case. Lord De Mallory! Oh, if you love me, don't mention the hob-goblin.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Hobgoblin! Is that a name for a husband?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Yes, I am afraid, a very common one—but as it is not an appellation I mean to bestow upon mine, I shall avoid making choice of Lord De Mallory.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: But how will you avoid it, my dear Lady?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Why, he can't marry me by main force, can he?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: I have heard of such things.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Have you indeed? Then I have a great mind to run away before he comes.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Oh, you wild thing, you!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I am resolved on it—Why all the right a poor woman has, (unless she be contented to live a solitary spinster) is to be a slave her own way. If I must have a lord and master, I am determined he shall be of my own choosing. Oh, I'll run away.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Run away, indeed! Where would you go? your brother you know is abroad.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Yes, yes, or I should not be at a loss where to go. He is my natural protector, and I am sure, would save me from the chains which his high mightiness, my old grandfather, forged for me. Oh, I'll run away.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Ha, ha! And what will you do when you have run away?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Any thing, sooner than be married against my will. Oh! I'll do a thousand things— Why, I'll—Lord! I declare, now I begin to think on it, I don't know what I should do.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Ah, you flighty creature! Well, well, in spite of all you say, I shall live to dance on my old knees, a pretty little baby of yours, that will call Lord De Mallory, papa.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Why then, I beg you'll whip him, for being a very story-telling little urchin. A baby of mine, call Lord De Mallory father! Why, I'd rather—What shall I say? I'd rather—never have a baby as long as I live.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Go your ways, go your ways, for a dear merry soul—Ah! Lord De Mallory you were a perverse boy to sour that sweet creature's mind towards you—but come, come, I will live in hope that you are grown a different being, and that the man is wise enough to prize a treasure of which the boy did not know the value.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: —A Park, with De Mallory Castle at a little distance.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: I say, Spruce,—have you looked me carefully over?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Yes, Sir Harry, very carefully.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: I'll take another turn tho', and mind now my good fellow, that you examine me strictly again.

div.stage: [Walks along for Spruce to observe him.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: All's right, Sir Harry, depend on it—Nothing about you that could move the muscles of the most confirmed joker in existence.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: That's well—for you know, Spruce, there is nothing too trifling, now-a-days, to make even a first-rate character an object of ridicule.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Very true, Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: A coat buttoned awry, or a knee-string left untied,
Oh, curse your carelessness—there, there—I am miserable man. You must have some base design, Sir, in such conduct—I see plainly you are plotting my ruin.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Really, Sir Harry, I am very sorry,—but indeed it must have happened by some accident.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: What if it did, Sir? The same accident did not take away your eye-sight—ah, Spruce, Spruce! will you never reflect, that a reputation a man has been labouring years to obtain, may all be blown into the air in a moment, by the infernal explosion of a damned horse-laugh!

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Pray, Sir Harry, be cool—all is right now.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Well, well, well—I am of a forgiving temper—But I say, Spruce—have you heard any of the family mention me?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: No, Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: What, really Spruce, in good earnest, you have not heard any little lively—damn'd coarse jokes made at my expense.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: No, indeed, Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: May be they are shy before you—Have you any reason to suppose they make free with me when you are out of the way? Do they wink much? That is a vile habit.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Oh, no, Sir Harry—never.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: And don't they whisper?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: A little, Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: The devil they do!

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Yes, Sir Harry—but I overheard—

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Well—what? Was it something very impertinent? Come, come—I am prepared—tell me the worst.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: You shall have it, Sir Harry—I overheard Mrs. Tattle say, that Lady Julia, her mistress, thought you—

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Quick, quick—What—what did she think me?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: A most accomplished gentleman.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: ‘Come, come—you are joking now.’

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: ‘Serious, Sir Harry—serious as when you are giving me a jobation.’

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Well—I always considered Lady Julia a girl of remarkable discernment. I must be particularly anxious to preserve this favourable impression. Of course, I can rely on your reporting me as you ought.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Oh, Sir Harry, can you doubt—

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: No—no—I don't—but there is a saying which I believe has some truth in it—that no man is a hero to his valet—but if that valet, Sir, is monster enough to make a jest of his master's little weaknesses—but there again, I am pretty secure— I am not aware, Spruce, of having any particularly weak points—am not in the habit of behaving very absurdly.—

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Oh, no, Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: To be sure, little mishaps will occur to every body—but they should never be hinted at— You'll be particularly cautious not to mention that unlucky event which happened to me last winter, in Parliament.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: What was that, Sir Harry?

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Oh—you never heard of it? Then don't mind, it is not worth mentioning.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Only, Sir Harry, that if it should be hinted at, I may be able, perhaps, to explain it away.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Then you'll succeed better than I did— I could never explain it away.—I thought to make a brilliant speech—subject matter all in my head— bursting with superabundant imagery—was three times called to order, for interrupting the member on his legs—at last he sat down—Now, whether his dull prose of three hours, threw a cloud over my imagination, or whether the dread of a failure, which unluckily popped into my mind, enfeebled me, I know not—but somehow my voice failed— my eyes grew dim—the chair vanished from my sight—and my utmost effort at articulation, could not get me so far as “Mr. Speaker”—My knees tottered, and down I sunk—with every sense but one suspended.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Which remained, Sir Harry?

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Oh, hearing, hearing, hearing! Never shall I forget the horrid sound. Billingsgate itself, with London Bridge to its aid, never equalled the roar of a senatorial horse-laugh.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: An ugly accident, indeed, Sir Harry—but I don't think it has travelled this road.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Ah! my dread of censure, certainly does cruelly maim the effect of my talents and accomplishments—Oh that birth-day faux pas has deprived me of a complete night's rest, ever since.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: How was that, Sir Harry?

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: What! is that, too, a secret to you? Oh, I am in better luck than I thought—Well, however, you shall know all, that you may strive to make the best of matters, if you should happen to hear my unfortunate failures mentioned with a sneer.—It has always been my ambition to figure away at a court ball; for there is nothing for which I am more celebrated, than my dancing.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: I know it, Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Well—the eyes of the whole room were consequently upon me—You may conceive the flutter it must give one, to have the attention of royalty fixed on one's performances—I acquitted myself, however, admirably, for a little time; but as the devil would have it, I somehow grew nervous, and gave the wrong hand for an allemande— From that moment, the game was up—I committed blunder after blunder—at last, my head spun— my heels flew up—down I went—and upset, in my fall, one Dutchess, two Countesses and a stiff little Lord of the bed-chamber.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Melancholy indeed, Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Horrible! It is the only time in my life, that I should have thought the loudest laugh a relief—but to my sorrow, I was in company, too highly bred for that—The awful silence that followed my mishap, was like a pause in nature— just like the stillness before a tremendous earthquake—Oh that the earthquake had followed, that I and my disgrace might have been buried together.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: It was distressing, Sir Harry; there is no denying it.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Distressing! Why, for months after, I never durst look into a newspaper, and I always shut my eyes when I came near a print shop.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Come, Sir Harry—you take little accidents too much to heart.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Too much to heart!—Why, I've often thought of retiring for comfort, into the back woods of America—There is nothing but torture in what is called civilized life. An ill-natured paragraph is worse than the arrow of an Indian, from behind a bush; and no tomahawk ever gave such a brain blow, as a caricature. Leave me, now, Spruce—I'll endeavour to compose myself and wait on the ladies

I believe I can depend on that fellow—if not, I am a most undone man. ‘It is melancholy that a being with my endowments, should be liable to such cursed humiliating accidents.’ Well, if I succeed with the fascinating Lady Julia, I shall then be an object of universal admiration, too elevated for ridicule to reach—No, no, no! Ridicule will bring down its game, let it soar ever so high—and now I think on it, I should not wonder if even the angelic creature, herself, should be made a jest of— Only fancy my idol, my divinity, the subject of newspaper sprites!—Oh, damn it! I'd be divorced.
Drive slowly up the avenue—I'll walk to the castle.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Whom have we here? I hate strangers. I'll avoid him.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Fair and softly, Sir—I see you are moving towards the castle—don't be in such a hurry and I'll bear you company.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: I don't know this old fellow—then what the devil can he see about me, to make him so cursed familiar? You are going to the castle, Sir?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Yes, Sir, I am. You are intimate there perhaps?

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: On a visit, may be—

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Yes, Sir. What a cross-examining old quiz.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! I can't help laughing.—

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: At what, Sir? at what? I don't see, Sir, how I should excite your mirth.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Nor I, upon my soul, Sir. I don't know what I may find you on further acquaintance, but you don't strike me as belonging to a society of jokers.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Sir, they are a set of men I abominate. ‘The wretches who used to live by vending poisons, were not half such pests in society.’ Like inquisitors, they roast their fellow-creatures for a merry making—they would sacrifice the feelings, the life, nay the reputation of their friends—and all for what, Sir? For the gratification of seeing a set of fools thrown into a damn'd ridiculous kind of convulsion.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Nay, nay, don't run down laughing, because like all good things, it is sometimes abused. Innocent mirth is the best of human recreations— Ay, and a fine medicine too,—it dislodges the bile better than Cheltenham Spa—A good joke comforts my heart; and I have such a regard for my health, that I never refuse to laugh even at a bad one. But I must explain to you, Sir, that my risibility, just now, was excited by the remembrance of the stately tribe that have stalked thro' life, in that mansion.—I'll be bound that not a soul of them, from generation to generation, was ever detected in any thing beyond a simper—Well! Rest them— merry, I was going to say—but that is impossible— they must be grand and melancholy, even in Paradise.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Curse the old banterer! Now am I ashamed to confess that I belong to a noble family, for fear of being quizzed for the stately gravity of my ancestors.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Not a word! Dull and dignified—I begin to smoke one of the house of De Mallory.
Do you know, Sir, I am inclined to suspect—

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: What, Sir? What?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Why, Sir, that you—

sp.speaker: Sir H
sp.p: What of me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I beg your pardon if I wrong you— The truth is, I shrewdly suspect you to be a shoot from the old Normandy crab, that William the Conqueror transplanted here.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Old Normandy crab!—Sir, it is true that I have the honour of springing from the noble stock of De Mallory.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I'd have betted a thousand upon it by your verjuice countenance. Ha, ha, ha! It is devilish odd, that in so many centuries, there should not be a little sweet fruit grafted on the sour old trunk.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Damn it! to have ridicule entailed on one, all the way from William the Conqueror, is rather too much.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Come, come—be patriotic—mend the breed—Look at me—I am a proof of what can be done in the way of improvement—You'll hardly believe that my mother was of your stock—but it is true. She, however, was so singular as to prefer comfort to dignity; and consulting her heart, instead of the Herald's Office, got a loving husband in lieu of a noble alliance—enjoyed domestic happiness, while her relations wasted life in cheerless state—and tho' her name never passed their proud lips, without condemnation, it was uttered with rapture, by her children, and with blessings, by the poor.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: I presume, Sir, your mother was Lady Gertrude Heartworth.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Yes Sir; and tho' lopped from your family tree, as a rotten branch, she took root in a soil more genial to her nature, and flourished in the sunshine of social felicity, diffusing the fruit of benevolence to all around her.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Sir, I am gratified to hear that her life passed so happily; and rejoice to meet in you, a relation that, I am sure will be welcomed as such, by the existing part of the family.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Give me your hand, Sir—it feels warmer than I ever thought to find the palm of one of my honourable cousins—that is, of the male side— for if I don't meet a loving squeeze,—ay, and a kiss, in the bargain, from my sweet Lady Julia Sandford, she must be much altered, and I shall be much disappointed.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Lady Julia! Then your visit is to her?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Who else, do you think? It is not the stately Dowager would have brought me from Cumberland—nor am I come to welcome the young Peer to England; for I understand he has all the faults of his ancestors, with a precious cargo of his own to boot—I am here, Sir, solely on Lady Julia's account, whom I met by accident, last summer; and who is the only one of the family, with whom I have any acquaintance. But, come, Sir, let us adjourn to the castle; and it is not unlikely that circumstances may very soon produce an explanation of the motives for my visit.

div.head: SCENE III.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Nay, nay, you are only jesting.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Well, well, you will soon be convinced.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: But are you really resolved to refuse the hand of Lord De Mallory.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Peremptorily.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: How you surprize me!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Lady De Mallory is by this time acquainted with my determination. Knowing the pride and violence of her disposition, I thought it most prudent to make the communication by letter.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: This is really very perplexing. You know my dear Julia how very much I am interested in this event.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: True my dear cousin. You will have to supply the vacancy I shall make in the marriage articles; and Harriet Alford must now follow all the aforesaids, behind which stood Julia Sandford.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: How distressing!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Why, you don't seem to have any greater inclination to this noble Peer than I have.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: She little thinks that the cause of my repugnance is an attachment to her brother.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: You have never suffered from his overbearing disposition, therefore cannot feel for him a dislike powerful as mine—but truly, Harriet, I must pity any woman destined to be his; and my love for you would make me pursue any measures to prevent your being his wife; short of becoming so myself. I see Lady De Mallory—she is seeking me—now for a storm, which as you may not much affect, you will be wise to retire.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: I will remain, if you think her anger will be moderated by the presence of a third person.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: No, my dear girl, nothing will soften her indignation; and you shan't suffer needless pain on my account.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Julia must not know my engagements to her brother, lest in her generous concern for us, she should involve herself in misery. No, I will encounter every difficulty sooner than owe my happiness to the sacrifice of her own.

div.stage: Lady De Mallory enters with two letters in her hand.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: You have filled me with amazement, child. Is it possible you can be so lost to every sense of duty and propriety?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I should be sorry your Ladyship could with justice, accuse me of being insensible to either.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: Such folly too! What! reject my son—the Lord De Mallory! you ought to consider yourself too happy in the mandate of your grandfather, which took from him the power of making another election.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Oh, how freely would I give him that power!

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: Ungrateful girl! Here in this letter from him, which I was reading with delight, when yours so unexpectedly poisoned my joy—here he acknowledges with gratitude, the pleasure your picture which I sent, has afforded him, and expresses the ardour with which he hastens to celebrate an union dear to him from inclination.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Madam, I can only regret that the inclination is not reciprocal.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: Come, come, dearest Julia, abandon this romantic opposition. I will confess that the manners of my son, when a boy, were somewhat repulsive: but why dwell thus on the errors of a child? Why should you conclude that reason and observation have not operated to remove his juvenile faults?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Because, Madam—Believe me, I am shocked to be compelled to speak such harsh truths to a mother;—Because, Madam, his faults were radical. He was tyrannical, where he never met opposition—he despised those who endeavoured by gentleness to conciliate esteem; and had no pleasure but from the compliance which was exacted by command.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: Very well, Madam, very well—I see your own imperious disposition is the real obstacle to your union with my son.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: You wrong me, Madam.—'Tis in nature for the gentlest being to resist oppression. I will not place myself in the power of a Tyrant; and therefore will never be the wife of Lord De Mallory.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: That is right, my girl! You shall not be the wife of a monarch against your will.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: And pray, Sir, who are you that volunteer thus, as the abettor of disobedience, in this house?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I am, madam, by inheritance, a kind of opposition member of this house.—I am not however one prone to argue against wholesome regulations and salutary authority.—But in a case like the present, where the freedom of election is in debate, here am I on my legs to defend privilege; and if the bill for compulsory measures be not withdrawn sine die, why then, Lady Julia we'll divide the house with them.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: What right have you, Sir, to interfere in a family arrangement?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Every Englishman, Madam, has a right to interfere for the prevention of oppression—but in this instance, I am particularly concerned, as the representative of one who was the innocent cause of this damned tyrannical family compact.—Because my mother chose to marry a worthy man, who had no deficiency but in his quarterings, this poor young lady is to be made the victim of wounded pride; and to be united to a man she dislikes, by the special license, forsooth, of an old grand father, long mouldered to dust—Confound such absurdity!

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: Sir, at once to put an end to an altercation, which I cannot consider but as highly offensive on your part, and the continuance of which it would be derogatory to my condition to suffer, I here state to Lady Julia, the terms on which, alone, she can experience the protection of this roof.—If she remain, it must be to ratify the will of her family, by becoming the wife of Lord De Mallory—Does she consent?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: No, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: She is then bereft of fortune, and these gates for ever shut against her.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Curse me, if one would not think, to hear that old dignified Dowager, that all the world was enclosed in the walls of this castle. Come, Lady Julia, let us be gone. As for a fortune, my girl, that I can give you, and if you grieve much at losing sight of these joyless towers, it can only be from a fondness for some pet owl you leave behind you.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Lady Julia, can what I hear, be true— that, to avoid marrying Lord De Mallory, you quit the Castle?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Yes; and if you are wise, you'll quit the Castle, too; for I would not have you trust too much to the protection of her ladyship's roof, which she makes such a rout about, for fear some stormy night it should be blown about your ears.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: You see I am a strange girl—many a young lady runs away to be married, but very few to avoid it.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Her leaving the Castle, must be all on my account that is very clear.
Pray, Lady Julia, may I be permitted to ask whither you are going?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Whither she is going? With me, to be sure.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: At least tell my Brother return to England, I shall place myself under the hospitable protection of this benevolent friend and relation.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: I hope I may be permitted to pay my respects to you.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: To be sure—Mine is Free and Easy Lodge—none of your Castle ceremonies at my house—You may go with us, if you like.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: May I? How happy you make me! But plague take it, what will Lady De Mallory say? Oh! I shall be scouted by the family, if I go with them.
No, no—If you please I will follow you—I have some arrangements here, unfinished.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Well, make haste—remember the old roof—I thought I saw a plaguy warp in one of the towers. Farewell.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Adieu
Her partiality for me is past all doubt.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Dear Lady Julia! and will you leave us?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I must, my good friend; or be miserable.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: I wish I had not lived to see this day. Ah! I shall never smile again.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: “Nay, good Randall, don't say so.”

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: “Ah, dear Lady! you have made sad hearts, and weeping eyes, throughout the Castle —but nobody has such cause for sorrow as myself. To be sure, you were good to every body; but you always treated me as tenderly as you could have done your own father; and for my part, I always loved you as well as ever I did a child of my own—But if you will be happier, we should not repine.”

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Come, child; or this good old man will set me whimpering.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Good bye, my dear old friend—We shall see one another, again.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Ah, my dear Lady! at seventy-five, a parting with those we love, is a serious thing. Well! be as happy as you are good, and I shall go to the grave contented.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Farewell!

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Heaven—Heaven for ever bless you!

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: Lord De Mallory and Major Clayton.

sp.speaker: Lord de Mallory.
Cl.
sp.p: We have reason to bless the hand of Nature for making islands. That salt ocean is a glorious preservative against corruption. We never need dread taint or decay, while the briny waves surround us.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: True, our insular situation is the protection of all that is dear to us. The ocean preserves us from the too easy influx of the specious underminers of morality, as well as the open foes of freedom.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Ah, my lord, as a peer of this country, how much more are you to be envied, than the greatest potentates of other lands! For you have rank and fortune to elevate and reward genius and virtue—your power to deal happiness to others is boundless, and your own happiness is secured by the laws, which restrain you from doing evil to any man.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Rightly said: for to him who knows how to appreciate a tranquil bosom, the prevention from doing evil must be esteemed the most valuable associate of power.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: My son!

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: My dear mother!

— Allow me to present to you this most valued friend, my companion, and best of monitors. To Major Clayton you owe the felicity of finding your son return to you so changed, as, I hope, never again to give you cause to blush for his conduct.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: I shall be happy to receive with the attentions due to his merit, a gentleman to whom my son expresses such obligations.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: I am honoured, Madam, far above my desert.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: But, mother, will not Julia, my destined bride, deign to welcome me? I hardly wonder at her coldness, for I don't know what perverse devil tempted me, but I always, though I loved her, used to be a sad torment to her.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: My Lord De Mallory must banish her from his thoughts.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Mother, you amaze me—Banish! I am at a loss to comprehend.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: She has rendered herself unworthy your consideration.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: What, Julia? How, for Heaven's sake?

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: She has quitted the castle, peremptorily disclaiming an alliance with your Lordship. Her avowed motives, forsooth, the remembrance of your acts of boyish tyranny.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: She had reason to hate me, but she has been too precipitate.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: All pretence, my Lord, such motives. Circumstances have thrown a new light upon her conduct.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Pray, explain.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: Your relation, Sir Harry Aspen, who came here avowedly to wait for your arrival, quitted the castle quickly after her departure.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: That may have been occasioned by other causes.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: The indiscreet tattle of his valet, has left no doubt on the subject—he not only communicated his master's route, which was to follow Lady Julia, but also discovered that he has been long attached to her.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Astonishing!

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: It was a fine deep laid plan. A Mr. Heartworth, an outcast of your family, came blustering here, to save her from oppression, as he termed it. He was evidently an accomplice, and took her away to avoid an open elopement with Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: This is an event I was not indeed prepared to meet.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: A very little reflection, my son, will make you bear it as you ought. You will soon rejoice at the prevention of an alliance so unworthy of you, and hasten to fulfil the compact of your grandfather, by a marriage with Miss Alford.—
sp.stage: (Lord De Mallory appearing surprised and going to speak)
sp.p: I will leave you now, my Lord.—After an event so unexpected, I know some little time is requisite to regulate the feelings; but yours will, I am certain, all concentre in self-respect, and regard for the honour of your house.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: An easy process it appears to her ladyship, to transfer a heart, like a clod of earth, to the next in succession. Julia's conduct wounds and irritates me—I wish her to feel that I am not a being she ought to have scorned.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Your Lordship's worth will soon make that clear to her—A nobleman's good deeds are seldom lost to the world for want of reporters.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Deeply wounded, both in my affections and my pride, I am anxious to seek a justifiable revenge.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: That, my Lord, is impossible to be obtained.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Because revenge is never justifiable.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Surely it is justifiable to endeavour to humble her pride, by letting her see the true character of the man she has rejected.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Oh! my Lord, never be rash enough to wage war with a petticoat. “There's magic in the web on't.” That garment will enlist more volunteers in its defence, than all the banners in the universe —it has more worshippers than all the relics of all the saints put together—it will animate and overthrow armies. Never hope to triumph over it—it is certain of conquest; for even if it surrender, it is only to enslave you the surer.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Say what you will, I am determined to pursue this runaway.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Begging your Lordship's pardon, it is a silly kind of chace, at best; and may turn out something worse. You hear she is attached to another. If her affections are so capricious as to veer round to you, I don't think you can much prize such a weathercock—then, what is your object?

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: To strive to convince her that at the same time she has forfeited her fortune by her choice, she has not been a gainer in the merits of her lover. If I can feelingly convince her of this, I shall with less regret devote myself to the other union prescribed me.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: I cannot see, my Lord, how your feelings are to be tranquillized by wounding those of another.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Hear me, Clayton. Though by your advice and example, I trust I have triumphed over the rough points of my character, yet I confess I do not wish to attain that degree of apathy which shall make me insensible of an injury.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: I have done, my Lord.—An argument strongly enforced in opposition to your Lordship's immediate feelings, raises a bulwark against conviction. Don't act precipitately, and I have no doubt of your acting rightly.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: To prove I always wish to be regulated by your counsels, let me entreat you to accompany me.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: That, my Lord, is at present impossible. I have an object that demands my immediate attention in another quarter—and let me hope that our pursuits may not prove of an opposite nature— That while my business is to dry the tears of a lovely woman, your Lordship may not give a lovely woman cause to weep.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: —Heartworth's House on the Lake of Windermere.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Well, dear Lady Julia, here you are, fixed on the banks of Windermere—and if you can make yourself tolerably happy in this simple abode, you will brighten my latter days.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Why, my dear Sir, this charming retreat is the very seat of happiness. Nature here wears her most romantic garb.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Inanimate Nature is to be sure in tolerable trim; but I fear the sons and daughters of the soil can afford you but little pleasure.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Oh! infinite—I am charmed with the variety I meet—each being has a character of his own, and talks and acts for himself—so different from the set to which I have been used, that aimed at being all alike, never thinking for a moment, whether what they did was right or wrong, pleasant or disagreeable, but only, was it the haut ton? Fashion, all-powerful fashion, can make infirmities, graces, dullness, high-breeding, and the sallies of a brilliant imagination be voted quite gothic.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Plague take the rage of imitation! which will make human beings, and very often, too, those of no mean intellect, place their whole pride in sinking into automatons.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Sir, Mrs. Leech wishes to see you.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Hey! what! Oh, the deuce—Well, well, tell her I'll wait on her presently.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I will ramble by the Lake, and leave you to your visitor.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Stay, stay, Lady Julia—You must know the—the—hang it! I dont know how to tell it you.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: What, my dear sir?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: We all have our plagues—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I am afraid that is very true.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I have a neighbour here—a lady—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: That—that—damn it! it is too ridiculous—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: What? What? You have raised my curiosity.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Who has most peremptorily made up her mind—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: To what?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Upon my soul, you'll laugh at me—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: No, no—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Why then—nay it is too absurd—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: You put me out of all patience.— What has she made up her mind to?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: To—to—to marry me.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: She is a very wise woman—I applaud her determination.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Pshaw, pshaw! no joking—mine is a devilish hard case—if I had given her encouragement—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: And are you very sure, now, you did not? I begin to be greatly afraid that you are a gay deceiver.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Psha, psha, psha! I just mentioned this foolish circumstance, or you might think her behaviour rather odd.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Ah, poor thing! she is clearly a deluded woman.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: But not by me, I'll swear.—What chiefly gave rise to this absurdity, was an unmeaning civility on my part.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Oh! now the murder is coming out.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: What the deuce! is the mere language of compliment to be taken literally?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Ah! there is the excuse of all you seducers.—You make fine speeches and tender professions—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Do I look like a maker of tender professions?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Oh, yes, very—and then if a poor woman is weak enough to credit you, you exclaim, “Oh, the silly creature! I meant nothing but badinage.—What I said was a mere façon de parler.”

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Why, plague take it! you may as well say, that when I subscribe myself a man's humble servant, it follows that he should send me his coat to brush or his shoes to clean—Does it give him a claim to my personal services.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: No—but when you profess yourself a lady's humble servant, it certainly gives her a claim to your personal services.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: But, you Mad-Cap, hear my story.—I went to console this silly old woman, five years ago, on the death of her second husband; and by way of comforting her, I just happened, unfortunately, to say that it would be her own fault if she remained a widow; for she might choose a husband whenever she pleased. The old fool took this unmeaning piece of civility for a declaration; and has thought fit to consider herself, Heaven help me! my wife elect, ever since.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Oh, you stony-hearted man, to hold out against such persevering constancy!

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Curse her constancy! If she would come plump to the point, I would set her right at once; but she never makes her attack direct enough for that—for these five years, has she been hinting and nodding and winking me into matrimony—and for aught I see, I may be doomed to a life of perpetual inuendo, till one of us drop to the grave.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: No, no—Depend upon it, she'll overcome her diffidence, and speak out at last—But how ungallant you are! Why don't you fly to her? Consider she is all impatience for a sight of her deary.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: But come, come—go with me.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Do you think I would spoil an agreeable tête à tête? The sight of me might damp all her joy; and I would not hurt her peace of mind, for the world. Now, be compassionate—Consider, true love is a jewel—Now, do force a little tenderness into your face, and strain your eyes into an agreeable ogle—Ha! ha! ha! Oh! you gay deceiver!

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Get along, Rattle Pate! Oh, I will bring this business to issue—I won't be tormented, and made ridiculous to boot, to humour any old woman in the universe—Plague take her, here she comes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: And am I so happy as to see you at home again, dear Mr Heartworth!

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Why, as to that—you see I am at home again, Mrs. Leech.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: How delighted I am to find it? Short as your absence has really been, I don't think I could outlive such another separation.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Oh, damn it, this is too much! I must speak out
not outlive a separation! Come, come, Mrs. Leech, that is very well of you—very well, indeed.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: The truth will burst forth.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Upon my soul, it is high time it should so, I shall speak plainly, and to the point.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: I knew I should draw out a full declaration at last.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I confess it is a delicate subject to talk about.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: A delicate subject! Yes, yes, all is now coming right.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I have, I confess, been foolishly shy, in not telling you my mind fully, before.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Oh, Mr. Heartworth!—Yes, now I may bespeak my wedding suit.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Oh! my dear Mr. Heartworth! I am all ecstasy to see you—Mrs. Leech, your most devoted—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Dr. Suitall, your servant.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: You gentlemen of a certain age, are the only gallants of the day. Ah! Mrs. Leech, this is a man indeed for the ladies.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Hey-day Doctor! What is the matter now?

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Such a charming thought! But mind, I must conduct the whole of the business.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: What business?

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Ah! you thought to be snug—but I've found out your devices. Haven't you heard of it, Ma'am?

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Of what Sir?

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Of a certain fête on the lake, which that gentleman is to give, in compliment to a lady.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: How delightful! With what gaiety he means to celebrate our union!
This is gallant, indeed, Mr. Heartworth.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Don't you think, Ma'am the lady must feel highly gratified?

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: That I am sure she does, Sir. Well, good morning, Mr. Heartworth—I must go and make preparations suitable to the approaching happy event. Good day, Doctor—Oh, I am quite fluttered with delight—Adieu.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: She will go and make preparations, will she? She might have waited first, for an invitation. You should not make such a fuss about this foolish water party.—I mean it as a little compliment to my cousin, Lady Julia, on her arrival here; but I don't want the people to imagine they are to see a Lord Mayor's Show.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Lord Mayor's Show! Why it shall beat the wedding of the Doge, if you'll let me manage it.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Stick to your physic, Doctor; leave the water to me.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: My physic won't be the worse for mixing water with it—Ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I never met such a fellow—water, fire, earth, air—you are never out of your element.
Ah, Sir Harry! Welcome, welcome—I see you are a man of your word.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: I lost no time in accepting your obliging invitation. How is the lovely Lady Julia?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Ah! there is the attraction—I shall find a vast addition to the list of my visitors. When I, a poor lonely humdrum old batchelor, used to send a card of invitation to only a few miles distance, I generally received for answer, that the badness of the roads, or the want of moonlight to return home by, prevented the extreme pleasure of waiting on me—Now, what a change there will be! The sight of my pretty cousin, will render the roads passable in all weather, without troubling the commissioners; and her bright eyes will make the moon shine every night in the month.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: This will be of great service to my shop —and give me leave to tell you, Sir Harry, that you need be under no anxiety about your health, while you remain in this neighbourhood. I am Doctor Suitall, dubbed, regularly dubbed—none of your Doctors by courtesy, though I do keep a shop—a shop you know is all the fashion. Besides, Sir Harry, you will find me at home, out of my shop—Ne sutor ultra crepidam, is not my motto. I know a thing or two, besides prescribing a bolus, and rolling it up.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Sir Harry won't be long without hearing, at least, of your universality.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: I am proud to be known to Sir Harry— Perhaps, thro' his high and extensive connections, I may entertain the hope of being removed from this limited circle, to a larger sphere of action.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: I am afraid, Sir, I have very little interest in forwarding a gentleman of your profession.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Don't let my medical profession, be a bar, Sir—I am a candidate for all sorts of employment. If you conceive, Sir Harry, that any such snug little appointment as Solicitor-General, nay a Puisne Judge, or even a Master in Chancery, should ever come within the pale of your recommendation, you'll find in your humble servant, a qualified person.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: What, Sir, to fill a great law situation?

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Most capably, Sir. I have legally fed both body and mind—ate my Commons at Gray's Inn, and have Coke upon Littleton, as completely by heart, as Cullen's Materia Medica.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: A most surprising man, indeed!

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Psha! that is nothing.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: True, true, Sir—nothing, indeed—Tam Marti, quam Mercurio—I trust you'll find me equally eligible to avail myself of your patronage, if your interest should happen to lie at the Admiralty or War Office.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: What the Devil!

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Yes, Sir Harry. Tactics, naval and military, have been favourite studies of mine; and that I might not lose an advantage for want of practical initiation, I have the honour of being a Brevet Lieutenant in the land service, and have served as Midshipman, on board the Atall Brig.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: This fellow must certainly be bantering me.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Here's Lady Julia; so, for the present, Doctor, I beseech you to remain contented with this very limited recital of your qualifications.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I am come, Sir, to claim your interference against an act of oppression.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Oppression! Eh! What oppression?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: You have promised a lease of Richland farm to—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Ay—to my neighbour Dawkins. The former tenant is dead, and has not left any family; so there is no oppression in that, surely.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Not on your part, Sir—but this man threatens to turn out of the cottage in which she was born, a poor woman who is old and helpless.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Eh! How did you learn this?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: From a lovely girl, her niece; who has left Wales, her native country, to assist this poor infirm relation.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: What can be the rascal's motive for such an act of barbarity?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: To frighten this sweet girl into a marriage with him.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Oh, the dog! So while I was gone to wage war at another man's castle, against a forced marriage, here was one of my tenants acting the same piece of oppression upon my own estate. Where is the fellow?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I've sent for him, Sir. In the mean time, let me present to you my little Welch protégée.

div.stage: Lady Julia goes off, and leads on Ellen.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: A lovely girl, indeed! Her pretty face, though it can excite a villain to an act of violence, will be sure to raise a host of champions to defend her.—So you were born in Wales my love?

sp.speaker: Ell.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: What is your name?

sp.speaker: Ell.
sp.p: Ellen.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Have you a father and mother?

sp.speaker: Ell.
sp.p: Oh! no, Sir—they are both dead.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Poor girl! What was your father?

sp.speaker: Ell.
sp.p: A soldier—who died in battle.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: What! have I lived to see the orphan of a soldier who died for his country, a victim of oppression? Grant me patience!

sp.speaker: Ell.
sp.p: My poor mother died but very lately—I was too young to live alone; so I came into these parts to seek my mother's sister—and I was glad I came, for her sake; for she was old, and very poor; and the little money I had, helped her much— and besides, I could work for her, and nurse her.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I'll have no mercy on the villain—he shall get off my lands; for I should expect an earthquake to swallow them, if I encouraged such monsters for my tenants.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: What a delightful part you have chosen, Lady Julia, to be the advocate of the oppressed!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: The oppressed need no advocate with a man like Mr. Heartworth.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Well, Lady Julia, we must contrive to provide comfortably for Goody Barton, and her pretty niece here; and if we can find my little Mountaineer a husband worthy of her, and whom she can like, Richland Farm shall be his.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: A worthy husband, and whom she can like! if I know any thing, it is the Art of Love— Richland Farm will be mine.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Come, Sir Harry, we will shew you a little aquatic fête, in compliment to our fair cousin.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: And we shall partake of amusement, now, with an increased zest, since it follows an act of justice and humanity.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: —The Lake of Windermere.—Pleasure Boats on it, decorated.—On Shore, Tents ornamented with Garlands, &c.

sp.p: I have arrived most opportunely.—This gala may prove the means of introducing me to Julia —Boy as I was when I left England, 'tis scarcely possible she should know me now. How full of emotion is my heart at the prospect of seeing her!

div.stage: Doctor Suitall enters with a Wand as Master of the Ceremonies.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Make room, make room, for the Master of the Ceremonies—Master of the Ceremonies by land—High Admiral on the waves—You smile, Sir,

You think waves, not completely correct, the lake being as smooth as glass—but poets, Sir, poets will speak in figure—You are a stranger, Sir, and know me not—but that I claim the title of bard, you will have the happiness of being assured, by my entreating your acceptance of two octavo volumes of miscellaneous poetry—you having the goodness to return, per bearer, thirteen shillings and sixpence—the price to original subscribers.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: I shall have great pleasure in perusing the works of a gentleman of whom, at first sight, I cannot but entertain a high opinion. This blockhead may be of service.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Clearly a man of discernment—he can certainly appreciate me—probably, promote me. Your name and connections, Sir, if you please.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Rather a home question, and what I am not exactly prepared to answer.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: He hesitates—Doubtless, a great man in disguise, who has heard of my great talents, and come to draw me from obscurity.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: I must answer him, or my silence will excite suspicion—I'll e'en use the name of my friend
Sir, Clayton is my name, and my connections—

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Whatever they are, Sir, they can't be amiss for me—Shew me how I can serve you, and depend on my using the same freedom, in return.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: I am a stranger, and anxious to participate in the present festivity—Oblige me by making me one of the party.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: It shall be done.—Stand away, there— make room, good people, for the Lord of the Manor.
Allow me to present to you, my particular friend —What did you say your name is?

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Clayton—Major Clayton.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: My tried and valued friend—Major Clayton.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I am glad to see you, Sir—I am a man of no ceremony—Come with us, and I hope you will pass a pleasant day.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: The honour of handing the Lady is my province.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: But where is my pretty Ellen.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: In yonder tent—when I have placed your Ladyship in the boat; I'll conduct her to you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: I am all of a flutter, I declare—I was afraid of being too late.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: I waited in anxious expectation of your calling to conduct me.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: You did?

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: It was not like your usual gallantry,
to let the lady in honour of whom you designed the gala, find her way to it, alone.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Hey?

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Why were you so remiss?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I was not.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Oh! then you meant to come for me.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: No, I did not.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Well, well, no matter. I am too happy to enter into argument. How delightful are your preparations! I declare I shan't be surprised if your charming entertainment in compliment to me, should gain me the title of the Lady of the Lake.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: In compliment to you!
The Lady of the Lake! Here, Lady Julia, do come and look at the Lady of the Lake!

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Lady Julia! Eh! what can all this mean?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: For goodness sake, dear Sir, don't expose the poor woman before all this company—Let her deceive herself a little longer— Do let her be the Lady of the Lake. Come, give the poor soul your hand.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I give her my hand!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Yes—to oblige me.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Oh, you coaxing jade! I can't deny you any thing—Come, Mrs. Leech.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: I really am at a loss to comprehend—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Don't expose yourself, you old—I beg pardon.—Mind, Lady Julia, this is all to oblige you; for if I had my wish, the Lady of the Lake, would be up to her neck in it’—Come along with with you—

div.stage: [he looks with dislike at her, and turns round to wink at Lady Julia.

sp.speaker: Doc.
sp.p: Lady Julia, your hand—Strike up, Music.

div.stage: [They enter the Boats as the Curtain drops.]

sp.p: So—this comes of pleasure-hunting! I must be drowning people, by way of amusement— Here, John! Thomas! No, not a soul in the house—all, on the water, or in it—Well, Doctor— good news I hope—

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: The very best—resuscitation has taken place—Major Clayton breathes again.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Then I shall begin to do the same— Ugh! my breath was gone, with terror. But for that dear girl, Lady Julia, your friend would never have seen daylight, more.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: She certainly was instrumental in his preservation.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Yes; for if she had not offered rewards for saving him, there would he have lain, till some drag-net caught hold of him—and as such an event might not happen for a week, or a fortnight, I fancy by that time, Doctor, even your galvanism would not revive him—but I thought you could do every thing—how comes it that swimming is out of the catalogue of your accomplishments?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Bless my soul! Don't imagine me deficient in any thing so essential—I swim like a salmon, float like a cork, and dive like a duck.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: And yet the pretty Ellen, of whom you pretend to be enamoured, slipt into the lake without your wetting a finger to save her—you left that service to your gallant friend; and when he plunged in, and, having lifted her to a boat in safety, sunk himself, exhausted, you still kept yourself as dry as a mouser; and seemed as much afraid of water as if you had got the hydrophobia.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Ah! ah! you are bantering—and you do it pretty well—bantering, is, probably, one of the things in which I most excel—but in fact, the omission you urge against me, arose from the variety of my excellence, for so many different ways of gliding through the waves rushed into my mind at once, that standing divided which to adopt—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Your mistress and friend would have been drowned, before you could decide.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: 'Tis a melancholy truth, that unthinking precipitation will sometimes bear away the palm from discriminating investigation.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Yes—and while your discriminating investigation was weighing the relative advantages of oxygen gas or tobacco smoke, for restoring suspended animation, your friend would have been as much beyond the power of revival, as an Egyptian Mummy.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: An Egyptian Mummy! well thought of —do you know, I understand the principles of embalming, as well as the first professor of the art, in the establishment of king Ptolemy.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: And I suppose you let your friends die, on purpose to keep your hand in.
Ah! my dear Girl, how is your Patient! Yours I may say; for to you he owes his life.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Repose, I believe, is all that is now necessary for his recovery.—Poor Ellen is so overcome by the fright she experienced, as to have strong symptoms of fever—Your aid, will, I fear, Doctor, be requisite.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: A fever!
I fly to her assistance.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Remember, now, what you are about— you are to preserve her alive, not dead—you may want to embalm her.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: No—I wish her to embalm me—in her heart

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Don't you think, Sir, that this is a most interesting man?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: What that damned Doctor, who professes every thing, and is fit for nothing?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: No, no—dear Sir—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Why, who do you mean?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Whom should I mean? The stranger, surely.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: The stranger! He interesting? Oh to be sure every body is interesting who is dragged out of a pond, or dug out of the snow—nay, I remember a fellow who was accounted as dull as a Dormouse, till he was cut down from a beam, to which the blockhead had tied himself; and ever after, he was considered a being of sensibility, and voted a most interesting creature.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: But surely you will allow that Major Clayton—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Is a noble fellow. Who will not allow it?—If a man venture his own life in the endeavour to save that of a dear friend, we admire his generosity —but, to him who will risk existence to preserve one whose only claim is that of being a fellow-creature, all mankind is debtor; and he that refuses to acknowledge the obligation, tacitly avows himself unworthy to rank as a human being.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I am certain this is no common kind of man.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I now remember that an officer of the name of Clayton, (whom I presume to be this gentleman) was reported in high terms for his professional character; and the circumstances relating to him, are pretty fresh in my mind. But here comes the Doctor—he introduced him—and will tell us whether this be the man.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Don't be alarmed about the lovely Ellen—With a little of my assistance, she will be speedily restored to the full bloom of health and beauty.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I rejoice to hear it.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Doctor, we are anxious to know whether your friend Major Clayton, is the same officer who behaved so gallantly at the taking of Seringapatam.

sp.speaker: Doctor.
sp.p: I have not the shadow of an idea.—Indubitably—the very man, He behaves gallantly, every where.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Of course, from your acquaintance with him, you have heard minute particulars of that glorious enterprize.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: The Devil a syllable.
Oh! no—he is a man of too much modesty, to talk over an action in which he was so eminently distinguished.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: That is like a brave man—I admire his silence—and that modesty is the surest path to renown—for when a man's own lips are closed to the recital of his exploits, every other mouth is ready to proclaim them; while the hero of his own tale, very soon becomes the only auditor.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Rightly observed, Sir.—I wish he would, drop this subject, for fear I should expose myself; for I don't remember a circumstance of the action to which he alludes.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: From the interest you must take in your friend's fame, you are doubtless, more possessed of the business, than I am—come, relate it to Lady Julia—she will be pleased to hear with what gallantry Major Clayton signalized himself; and, for my part, I could listen for ever, to the glorious achievements of my countrymen.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Here is a dilemma! I am to render a faithful and clear account of an action of which I don't know a single particular, in the hearing of a man who has every Extraordinary Gazette by heart—there is only one way left for me—so, impudence assist me
—The action, to the best of my recollection, began—
let me see—I wish to be accurate—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: At one o'clock, in the day.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Precisely.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Then the troops moved from the trenches.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Yes; the troops moved then from the trenches.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Crossed the rocky bed of the Cavery.—

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Pressed forward—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: And, under a tremendous fire, passed the glacis and ditch—

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Only think of that, Ma'am—passed the glacis and ditch!—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Ascended the breaches in the fausse braye and rampart of the fort—

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Observe what I tell you Lady Julia—the rampart of the fort—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Surmounting, in the most gallant manner, every obstacle—

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Mind, Ma'am—every individual obstacle, and—and—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: And success was complete.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Success, you see, Madam, complete. I am pretty accurate, you find, Sir—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Yes, yes—but your friend Major Clayton.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Ay, Madam—now you shall hear of my friend, Major Clayton—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: You remember when his Colonel was disabled, and surrounded by the enemy, how the Major—

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Yes—there was a display for the Major's gallantry?—When his Colonel was surrounded by the enemy—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: He cut through the whole mass of them—

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Thro' the whole mass.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: And bore him off in safety.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Off in safety—Victoria! Victoria!

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Give me your hand—I laud your enthusiasm. May the British arms, in every contest, meet with the same glorious issue!

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Off in safety, Madam—Victoria! Victoria!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I remember I used to shrink from the recital of such events; and now I could listen for ever. Ah! 'tis the hero of the story, excites this interest—Oh dear, how oddly I feel! Why should not I be cheerful? He is restored to life—he is out of all danger—he—he! why, heaven defend me! I can say nothing but he— Who's this?—as sure as fate, 'tis he—Oh, what a flutter I am in!

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: I was full of anxiety, Madam, to meet you.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: You should not have left your chamber so soon—you require repose.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Was it possible to find repose, with such a debt of gratitude unpaid, as that I owe to you? To you I am indebted for my life—accept such thanks—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Oh! cease—I can't bear to receive thanks from one whose generous zeal in the cause of humanity, demands the thanks and admiration of all.—Pray, spare me.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: I am inclined to obey you; but only because I feel inadequate to thank you as I ought—When the heart beats with the strongest feelings, the tongue is often least able to execute the office of expressing them. Only let me say the life you have saved, should with ardour be sacrificed, to promote your happiness.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Sacrificed! Oh! no—it must be carefully preserved, to promote my happiness.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: And may I, Lady Julia, at least, be allowed to think that while your tenderer, warmer, sentiments are devoted to another.—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Another! I don't know where that other gentleman lives, I am sure.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: You will deign, sometimes, to remember him who will for ever cherish you, as the dearest object of his gratitude—the only object of his—love.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Sir! Did I hear rightly? Did you say—I must mind what I am doing—I am so delighted—but I must be prudent—I shall seem forward, I fear—Love! Yes, he did say, Love— I—I—I am so agitated
Oh, help! A chair!
sp.stage: (Lord de M. offers to take her in his arms)
sp.p: No, no,—not your arms—a chair, a chair!
sp.stage: (While Lord de Mallory runs for a chair, Sir Harry Aspen enters, and catches Lady Julia, who is fainting, in his arms.)

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Not in my arms!—No, no,—Those are the arms—If I remain, I shall not control my indignation. Oh Julia!—Distraction!

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Delicate creature!—Not his arms— No, no—She would not faint in any arms but mine.—Ah! She evidently saw me approaching.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: You are very kind—I can't think what affected me so—You see I needed your support, though I rejected it—

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: From another. Oh! Lady Julia, I am flattered beyond—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Sir!
sp.stage: (looking at him with surprize, and then looking round)

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: I must not be too abrupt, I find; ‘otherwise she'll think it necessary to give herself airs; and that would throw me into a ridiculous situation.’

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I hope, Sir Harry, you will not misconceive.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: I, Madam! Impossible.—No, no— there is no danger of that—it is all too plain to be misconceived

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I fear a return of my indisposition—I must retire for air.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Poor dear! A strong case, indeed.— Do me the honour to accept my assistance.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I don't need it, Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: I hope, Lady Julia, you will soon recover this—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Oh, yes—no doubt—good day, Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: My most fervent wishes for your health.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Good day, Sir Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Poor thing—agitated beyond description—Before she leaves the pleasure grounds—I will summon resolution, and declare my passion— My success here will make ample amends for all my failures—Bravo, Sir Harry! You have done wonders indeed.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: A part of Mr. Heartworth's Pleasure Grounds.
Mrs. Leech enters with Doctor Suitall.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: I know, Doctor, I can speak to you as a friend—do you really think that Mr. Heartworth retains his tender partiality for me?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Just as much as ever.—Strict truth, that —for he always voted her as nauseous as Ipecacuanha.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: I really began to fear that this fine lady of fashion, his relation, forsooth! had alienated his affections.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Not dislocated a joint of them.—Oh! Mrs Leech, you are forgetful of your own charms.—Must dose my patients with flattery, or they wont let me dose them with any thing else.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Mr Heartworth is certainly very much altered, since his visit to De Mallory Castle.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Altered! What—looks older, you think?

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Older? No—what I mean, is, that he is a great deal prouder—but he should consider that other people have high connections, as well as himself.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Bless my soul—here's a discovery! high connections!
My dear Mrs. Leech, what can I do to serve you? Command my heart, soul, tongue, pen, sword, and shop—did not you just hint something about high connections?

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Yes, to be sure—I have a brother a General Officer.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Very good—stop, stop—Brigade Major, will do vastly well for me.
Go on, if you please.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: And a first cousin an Ambassador.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: You need say no more—you have hit it—if I have a talent, it is diplomatic—Secretary to an Embassy—Chargé d'Affaires—huzza! I am a made man, at last—now only tell me how I can serve you—I'll insist on Mr. Heartworth's marrying you—Chargé d'Affaires! Oh! that will screw me up to any thing—I'll marry you myself, if you like.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: What did you say, Doctor?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: I said—that is—I was thinking that— w'ell at all events try Mr. Heartworth first— marry her myself! No, no—that bolus need not be swallowed till all else fail—I'll reserve that desperate sally for a forlorn hope.

My dear Mrs. Leech, I fly to serve you—you could not put your case into the hands of a better special pleader—I'll board him so stoutly, that if he don't strike to you, may I never be honoured with a smile from a Prime Minister!

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: One would imagine, indeed, that a man at Mr. Heartworth's time of life, might think himself too happy to be honoured with the hand of a woman like me—but now a days, the old are as much given to roving, as the young—Well, Mr. Heartworth, if you should be blind to your own good, you shall find, at least, that I am not reduced to the last extremity—somebody is approaching—doubtless, Mr. Heartworth—this is his favourite walk—I'll step into this arbour— there is something sentimental in an arbour— there he shall find me reclining in an elegant, captivating attitude; and if he should chance not to espy me, a few tender sighs shall indicate my retreat.

div.stage: [Sir Harry Aspen enters, as Mrs. Leech is going into the arbour, and just sees the train of her gown.]

sp.speaker: Sir. H.
sp.p: Yes, there is Lady Julia—she seats herself at my approach—that, very plainly says.— Sir Harry, I am not disposed to avoid you—courage Chevalier! Now is your time to speak—

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: A tender sigh! Very well—If you needed farther encouragement, Sir Harry, there, I think you have it. Had I better go into the arbour, and seat myself by her side, at once? No, no—that, I think, will be too abrupt—notwithstanding her evident passion for me, she is devilish high; and her pride may take the alarm at any thing she considers presuming—no—this is the plan—
sp.stage: [takes a garden chair, and draws it close to the arbour.]
sp.p: How shall I begin?

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Another! I am afraid she will begin to think me very tardy—well, now for it.
I—Madam—my passion—your charms—Oh! curse it! here will be another failure—rally your spirits, my dear Sir Harry.

Permit me to say, Madam, I—I—I—love you to—to desperation—I would not see her face, now, for the world; ‘for if she feel it necessary to look indignant, I should never be able to open my lips again, as long as I live.’

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: That will do—it is all right.

You may judge my misery when I had reason to dread your marriage with another—that apprehension being removed, give me leave to hope that my fervent affection will not be treated with indifference—bravo, Sir Harry! I think I might venture to meet her looks, now.
Oh, deign, then, loveliest of women, to behold your adorer at your feet!

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: There is no resisting this—the hardest heart would melt—oh, Sir Harry!

div.stage: [Comes out and throws herself on his neck.
Heartworth, Lady Julia, Lord De Mallory, and Dr. Suitall, enter.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Well done, widow!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Sir Harry!

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Lady Julia there!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Yes; and I humbly entreat your pardon for interrupting so exquisite a love-scene.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: Why, Lady Julia—why Madam—

div.stage: [Heartworth, Lady Julia, and Lord De Mallory, laugh.

sp.speaker: Sir H.
sp.p: This is beyond endurance—I am ruined —the game is up with me, for ever—I'll never see day-light again—nor a human countenance. I have not a hope left—no consolation in nature— Yes, yes, I have—for there are such comforts still in existence, as flint and steel, and a powdermill.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: How he takes the discovery to heart! Why, widow, how much better you bear it! Oh! I suppose you are used to discoveries.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Don't be scurrilous, Sir.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Mrs. Leech, just permit me to say, that you have not paid a proper respect to delegated authority—you invested me with power to negociate a treaty in one quarter, while you were ratifying a very close counteracting alliance in another—This is conduct at which, I am sure, your cousin the Ambassador would feel highly indignant—but I won't reprove you harshly, because I never lose my respect for persons of high connection.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Well, widow, at all events, you will now give up your claim on me—I am fairly exonerated.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Certainly, Mr. Heartworth. The man who trifles with affection, can never, with reason, complain of its being transferred to another; and when you compare the pretensions of the two objects in question, you cannot, I think, fail to admit, that a woman must possess very limited powers of discrimination, who would hesitate where to give the preference. Good day, Mr. Heartworth, you will excuse me I hope.

sp.speaker: Doct.
