sp.p: I doubt whether her brother the General, could have made an abler retreat. Oh! there is a deal of the old soldier about her. I'll bring up her rear however—for if she is at issue with me, I must administer my specific sedative, adulation— that she may put in my plea with her cousin the Ambassador—Chargé d'Affaires, must never be lost sight of.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Why, what the plague, can this mean? Is Sir Harry frantic? I thought he had a hankering kindness for you.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I never perceived it—but if that were the case, I suppose he was resolved to pique me for my insensibility, by convincing me that all women are not equally blind to his accomplishments.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I'll follow the poor fellow, however; for since he is so mad as to fall in love with the widow, he is desperate enough to do any thing.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Is it possible, Lady Julia, that Sir Harry never declared a passion for you, or received encouragement.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Encouragement from me!—Sir Harry receive encouragement! Never.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: By this avowal you have given me life a second time.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: How could you conceive any thing so totally unfounded?

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: Pardon my absurdity—I blush to think that I should have been the dupe of scandal.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I am shocked to think that I should be the object of it.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: 'Tis the tax which superior excellence must pay to envy.—You have relieved me, Lady Julia, from the pangs of hopeless love— while your heart is not devoted to another, I will cherish the dear idea that you may be mine. Oh! give me the happiness of hearing from your own lips, that I am not hateful to you!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Hateful is a strong word—no, no— indeed, you are not quite hateful to me.

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: On my knees, let me thank you for your goodness.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Hey-day! Pray, are you amusing yourselves by acting Sir Harry and the widow, or are you making love for yourselves, good people?

sp.speaker: Lord De M.
sp.p: To you, and to the whole world, I am ready to avow my ardent passion for Lady Julia—and Lord De Mallory, now,

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Lord De Mallory! Don't mention that name—Lord De Mallory has on right here—and if you are even an acquaintance of his Lordship, it may be sufficient to ruin your chance.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: I have to inform you, Major Clayton, that, having purchased my freedom with the loss of my fortune, Lord De Mallory can claim no interference with me: so circumstanced, all mention of him must be unnecessary; and when I tell you that his very name is odious to me, I trust you will forbear to repeat it.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: There now, you find I am right—If you are a friend of Lord De Mallory's cut the connection.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: How violent the prejudice! I shall be ruined if I avow myself.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Major Clayton, give me your hand.— Damn Lord de Mallory—I like you as much as I hate him—ay, and my cousin Julia likes you, too, whether she have told you so, or not.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: My dear Sir, you go too far.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Do I? Well, I shall mend that fault by going a great deal farther. I am a plain fellow, that come plump to a point at once—There stands Lady Julia Sandford, to whom, as respectable a Banker as ever Lombard Street produced, is ready to pay, on demand, the sum of twenty thousand pounds—This trifling circumstance being premised, I take the hand of the aforesaid Lady Julia, and consign it to Major Clayton, as a pledge that the Parson, shall cement the union to-morrow morning.

div.stage: [Heartworth takes Lady Julia's hand—She just sufficiently reluctant, to accord with female delicacy— Lord de Mallory starts back.]

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: What the devil do you shrink at?—Oh! I dare swear you have got into your head, some confused notion that we shall make enquiries into your rent-roll, for which you may not be quite prepared—No, no, we are different kind of people—we know better—a soldier's rent-roll is the record of his gallant deeds—and yours, Major Clayton, is of higher value in my estimation, than the fee-simple of a whole country.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: I am distracted!—Despised as myself—valued only for the merit of the character I have assumed!—Accept her hand as an impostor? Impossible! I should be the most degraded of beings.

div.stage: [Heartworth and Lady Julia, look with astonishment at his hesitation.]

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: While I possess a particle, in my composition, of such an ingredient as patience, allow me to ask, whence this extraordinary conduct proceeds?

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: I can, at present, give no explanation—The treasure offered me, constitutes all I wish on earth—yet I must—distraction!—Lady Julia, pity me—do not hate me—Suspend your sentence on my conduct—By Heaven, I will not prove unworthy of you—Time shall clear all—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Whew—whew! I have exposed myself—I am a fool—a cursed old fool— “Time shall clear all”! shall it? I dare say—It is—it is, as clear as day—This damned fellow has got a wife somewhere, and when he has poisoned her, or cut her throat, he will then be here again, to marry you—Oh, Julia, forgive me! I am a precipitate old blockhead, easily imposed on by a specious appearance, and blazing reputation—A plague on all Gazettes!—I'll never read another— Forgive me, my dear girl,—do, pray, forgive me!

div.head: SCENE I.

sp.speaker: Doctor Suitall.
sp.p: Lean hard—you must be a little faintish, but you look bloomingly, you do great credit to my medical skill. But let us now “throw physic to the dogs.” “Let us talk of war”—your father was a soldier?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: You naturally love a soldier?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Good. I am one—Brevet Lieutenant. Any friends in the navy?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: No, Besides those you know of, I have no friend, but one,
any where.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: But one friend.—Rather scantily appointed. Well, one friend may do something.
Allow me to inquire who that friend may be?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: 'Tis no matter.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Oh, ho! close on the subject—a friend in a corner—well, a friend in a corner frequently makes a family thrive prodigiously. Sorry her connections are so limited—but she is really very pretty; and I don't know any of my professions in which a pretty wife has not been the cause of promotion.—But I must come to the point.
My charming patient, tell me—have not you felt a certain sensation called—

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Love.

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Oh, yes!

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: You feel it now, may be?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Yes;—and shall, as long as I live.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: I knew it—I knew it—Doctor you are a deluding rogue—you never fail. Ha! here is Lady Julia.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: My dear Ellen, I rejoice to see you so perfectly recovered.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: You do me great honour.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: How do you make out that?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Bless me! is not her perfect recovery a proof of my skill?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: That's by no means clear; but I will allow you one merit—letting her recover so soon is a tolerable proof of your honesty.

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Pray, Madam, where is the gentleman who saved my life?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: At your elbow, to be sure.

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: I mean the gentleman who snatched me from the lake. I wish to tell him I am not ungrateful.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: He is no longer here.

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: No! I am very sorry—I am told, that by saving me, he was almost drowned himself—Oh! what a generous, good man!

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Generous—good—he is the greatest scoundrel in existence.

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Calm yourself, dear Sir!

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: And you—are not you a pretty fellow to introduce such a villain?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: My dear Sir, consider the Extraordinary Gazette—One would have thought Major Clayton's being a villain impossible.

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Major Clayton! yes, yes, that is impossible.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: What an animated defence! oh, ho! the friend in a corner, to a certainty.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Do you know Major Clayton?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Oh, yes, I do know him.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Poor thing! to your cost I dare swear. Ay, ay, I warrant he has an extensive acquaintance among such pretty girls as you.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: How came you to know him?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: I'll tell you, Madam. My father served with him in India; and, when he lost his life, at the taking of Seringapatam.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Was your father at the taking of Seringapatam?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: His name?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Meredith.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: How! the brave serjeant who was mortally wounded in the defence of his commanding officer?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: Yes, Sir; and that officer was Major Clayton.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: What do you tell me, your father lost his life in defending this man, who, as I guess, has been to you—

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: A second father!—oh, Sir, he has been everything to me.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Curse it, I was afraid so!

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: As soon as he came to England, he hastened to comfort my poor mother and myself.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: A precious comforter!

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: He provided us with every thing we could desire; and, tho' I was in so humble a station, and he so great, yet he promised—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: To marry you, I dare be sworn. The old trick!—Yes, yes—I knew how this would end; and you expect, no doubt, that he will keep his word?

sp.speaker: El.
sp.p: If he is alive, I am sure of it.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Bless your poor deluded heart! Take my advice, get a plain, honest husband as soon as you can; and think no more of your Major than he thinks of you.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: She weeps—poor dear! I am ordained to dry those tears—not her first love it appears— no matter—a second choice is a proof of amended judgment. Sir
tho' I am not exactly of the description you recommend,—a plain honest—

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: What, you admit you have not any such pretensions.—To say the truth, I don't see how you can, for as there is supposed to be a little roguery in every profession, your sum total of honesty, must experience a multitude of drawbacks.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: A stranger, Sir, wishes to see you.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Is this another friend of yours? Damn all strangers! we have had enough of strangers.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: What shall I say to him, Sir?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Tell him—no, no—don't let me become a brute, because I have met a rogue.—Tell the gentleman to walk in.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: We will retire.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: And so will I, too, till I know his errand—I am sick of strangers—Doctor, I will turn him over to you, and if he prove a scoundrel, then, you know, we shall be quit on the score of introduction.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: With all my heart. A man like me who solicits an extensive connection, must not be too scrupulous. Lady Julia, your most devoted. Miss Ellen, though, like Ariadne, deserted by a faithless Theseus—don't despair, I will be the jolly god, Bacchus, at your service.
Poor dear! all heathen Greek to her—I must give her a smattering of mythology.

div.stage: (Servant ushers in Major Clayton and exit.)

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Sir, your most obedient—my friend Mr. Heartworth has consigned to me, the honour of receiving you. May I beg to be favoured with your commands?

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Sir, the motive for my intrusion, is to inquire after a lovely orphan, whom, I find, he has humanely taken under his protection.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Her name, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Ellen Meredith.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Oh—an object of general pursuit, I see— her connections will multiply amazingly—I must make her my own, with all expedition.

Sir, I have the pleasure of informing you that she is well, which happy event is entirely owing to the transcendent skill of a certain person who shall, at present, be nameless—and this same highly gifted, highly qualified, personage, who led her to the temple of Health, will shortly, lead her to the temple of Hymen.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: And who, Sir, may this be?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: One, who, when he has the honour of Miss Ellen's hand, will be proud to solicit your good offices.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Sir, what does all this mean?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: You are in the dark, I find—I'll illumine you.—You must know, Sir, that this angelic creature was first over head and ears in love—then over head and ears in the water—and the same gentleman who plunged her into the first dilemma dragged her out of the second.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: And who is this gentleman?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: You shall hear all anon, Sir.—Then followed a fever, which was speedily routed.—Health restored, there was no longer need of the doctor, who then transmuted himself into a lover, and has now the honour of presenting himself to your notice and patronage, in the several capacities of, Doctor of physic, Bachelor of civil law, Barrister at common law, Brevet Lieutenant in the army, and Midshipman on board the Atall brig—with more et ceteras than the oldest peer of the realm.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: And you, Sir, are to be the husband of Ellen?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: I trust so, Sir,—that is, if her first love fit prove perfectly pure and Platonic—otherwise, my honour, civil and military, forbids the banns.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: And, who, Sir, is this lover you speak of?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Oh, a great rogue—he has made sad havock here, in another quarter, too.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Indeed! His name, Sir?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: If I confide it to you, you will, of course, not mention I called him a rogue; for it is my practice never to make an enemy—particularly of a brave man.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: I will be secret.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Between ourselves, though, he is a most complete scoundrel.—His name is Clayton.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Sir!—What Clayton?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: What Clayton? The Clayton—Major Clayton, who fought so bravely at Seringapatam.— You would not have thought him such a rogue, would you?

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: And are you certain, Sir, of the truth of your assertions?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Absolutely.—Mind, now, I would not have Major Clayton know what I tell you, for the world; but still, I assure you, he is clearly the most consummate villain—
sp.stage: (going close, and looking him in the face.)

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.stage: (In a very loud and determined tone)
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Bless my soul! What is the matter?

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Have you ever received the punishment due to consummate falsehood?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: I? Lord, no—why should I? I never told a lie in my life.—You'll observe, though I am called to the bar, I have never practised.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Sir, you have traduced an innocent girl; and calumniated a man of honour; but you shall not escape the chastisement you merit.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Heyday! What is all this? Chastisement! why, Doctor, this new connection is not likely to ripen into friendship.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: No—though I certainly cannot upbraid the gentleman with treating me coolly.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Yet, notwithstanding, I think he keeps you at an awful distance.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: You, I presume, Sir, are Mr. Heartworth. I am sorry to have been urged to such warmth under your roof.—Can you account, Sir, for the conduct of this man, in vilifying an innocent girl whom you have thought worthy of your protection?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: He vilify! He did not dare, sure?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Bless you! I never thought of such a thing. I only hinted at Ellen's acknowledged affection for Major Clayton.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: I am sorry to state that to be a fact, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: And why should you lament her attachment to a man of honour?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Ah! damn it, Sir, you have been deceived, like me, by the Extraordinary Gazette.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: That is the fact, Sir—Our little misunderstanding has been all owing to the Extraordinary Gazette.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Gentlemen are you in your senses, or have I lost mine? What has Major Clayton done, inconsistent with his general estimation?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Oh—I will soon settle his estimation in your mind—You think you can defend him?

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: I am certain of it.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Very well—we shall see.—In the first place, seducing the affections of an innocent girl in humble life, under a promise of marriage, is, I presume, a mere bagatelle—a ruse de guerre—an allowable military manœuvre?

sp.speaker: Cl.
Heart.
sp.p: Give me your hand, Sir;—I always despised those fellows who purchase the title of men of gallantry at the expense of every quality that constitutes a man of honour.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Then, Sir, as Major Clayton is a man of honour, he cannot have acted as you describe.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: But I assert he promised marriage to Ellen Meredith.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Which promise, he will most religiously perform.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Will he?—Then, Sir, I have you in a cleft stick—If that be his intention, how did he dare make his addresses to a woman of rank, under my protection,—Lady Julia Sandford?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Ay, Sir,—how do you account for that? We shall pose this defender clearly.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Make his addresses to Lady Julia Sandford! He never beheld Lady Julia Sandford.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Oh, come, come—have done, have done.—Eh! Doctor, we are to be cajoled out of our senses, I see—Here stands the very man who introduced him.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: 'Tis a melancholy fact, Sir—I was the unfortunate agent—

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Of the devil, it should seem, by your enormous falsehoods. Be assured that shame will quickly reach you—But to the purpose of my visit— 'Tis to see Ellen Meredith.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Sir, I must know you better before I consent to that.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: You are right. Stick to that point—He is a terribly dangerous fellow. If there were a Phœnix-Office for insuring female virtue, an acquaintance with a soldier would be excepted against like combustible matter, and no more within the intent of a policy, than a powder-mill.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Sir, my right to see Ellen Meredith is indisputable, and—

sp.speaker: Ellen
sp.p: I heard my name—and from a voice—
ah! it is he—it is Major Clayton! —

sp.speaker: Doct. and Heart.
sp.p: Major Clayton!

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.stage: (looking first with great surprise at Major Clayton, and then turning, with ludicrous indignation, to the Doctor, who retreats—Heartworth following him.)
sp.p: And, pray, Sir, what sharper of your acquaintance did you introduce to me as this gentleman?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: What shall I do? all is up with me here, I shall never get another customer.—Sir, I have been imposed upon—advantage has been taken of my credulity—but I will have redress—I will follow the impostor through the world—He has destroyed my practice as a Physician, and I will be revenged as a Lawyer. He has injured my reputation as a man, and I will have satisfaction, naval and military—I'll challenge and I'll capias him—I'll change into every shape, to pursue him.—If I find he is in debt, damn it, I'll turn bailiff, to have the pleasure of arresting him.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Contrive to get him for a patient; he'd be in most danger from your physic. Let me welcome you, now, Major Clayton, as your merits demand; and pray forget, if possible, the inhospitable reception you have experienced.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: It was owing to mistake, Sir; and, therefore, does not require the slightest consideration. And now, sir, accept my warmest thanks for the protection you have afforded this lovely girl.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: To protect the orphan, Sir, is the common duty of a man; but, to relieve every one from oppression, is an English gentleman's province— 'tis a debt he owes for his own felicity; and, besides, the best security for the independence of his mansion is, to see freedom flourish in the cot beneath it. All that is dear to himself must be well defended, when the lowest man in the ranks has rights of his own to maintain.

div.stage: Randall and a Servant of Heartworth's enter.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: I hope, Sir, you ben't a stranger?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Why so, friend?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Because, if you be, I would rather not mention that you are here.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: No! why?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: My master, somehow, doesn't fancy 'em much. When I told him, this morning, there was a stranger wanted him, what do you think now he said?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: I am sure I can't tell.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Why, he said, “Damn all strangers—we have had enough of strangers.”

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: But I want to speak to Lady Julia; and I am no stranger to her.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Oh, I should not mind if you were; for I have not heard her damn strangers yet. Well, I'll tell Lady Julia a friend wants her.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: No, no—that is too familiar—not a friend—

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Not a friend! oh, but I might have known that; for a friend is a stranger, almost every where.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Tell her, her old faithful Randall wishes to see her.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Old faithful Randall? Yes, I will tell her so—old Mr. faithful Randall.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: How I long to see the dear creature once again!—I thought I should have been more fatigued by my journey; but even old age feels little toil, when the mind is intent on the pleasure of beholding an object it loves. Ah! here she comes.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: My dear good friend, how glad I am to see you!

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: The sight of you, my sweet Lady, makes me young again. I am come all the way from De Mallory Castle, to fetch home a truant. You surely won't break my heart by refusing to return.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Nay, dear Randall, why do you urge what you know I must deny?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: ‘No, no, you won't deny, when you hear what I have to say. Lord De Mallory is the most altered creature—he is the gentlest, the most amiable—’

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: ‘Ah! you have strong partialities.’

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Do not ‘you Lady,’ persist in prejudices, when the cause which inspired them ceases to exist. Your brother feels the warmest friendship for Lord De Mallory, and—

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: My brother! Is my brother returned to England?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Yes—and I fear your conduct has been misrepresented to him.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: How misrepresented?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Forgive me if I tell you painful truths. Your leaving the castle has been imputed to motives beyond aversion to a marriage with Lord De Mallory. Sir Harry Aspen is believed to be a favoured lover.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Can this be possible?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: It is; and therefore I came hither to beg you to return, to vindicate your reputation. I have been as loud in your defence as my old lungs would let me. It almost made me frantic to hear you taxed with artifice, whom I know to have a heart all openness and innocence.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Thanks, good Randall! However painful it is to me to return, I owe it to my honour, and must and will assert myself. It is the fashion to hear friends traduced, with the most well-bred apathy; and to be warm in their defence, is deemed a boisterous violation of the harmony of civilized scandal. You exhibit an amiable contrast to such unfeeling refinement; and shame on all those who, unlike yourself, suffer a reputation to be sullied, without asserting the cause of truth; and who meanly purchase the character of polished forbearance, at the expense of man's noblest attribute—zeal for the vindication of innocence!

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: —An Apartment in the Castle of De Mallory.
Lord de Mallory and his Mother.

sp.speaker: Lord De Mallory.
sp.p: So that, my dear Madam, all you have heard of Lady Julia's conduct is erroneous. I assert her innocence, and am both proud and happy in the assurance that she loves me.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: Her flying from the castle at your approach is a convincing proof of it.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: She was justified in avoiding me. My boyish insolence, my unwarrantable impetuosity, authorized her former dislike to me; but that has subsided with the cause of it, and my corrected disposition has converted repugnance into affection.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: Well,—granting her affection—is your honour to be sacrificed to that fluctuating caprice, called love? Had your ancestors consulted such feelings, instead of their dignity, young might not now be possessed of the proud titles which distinguish you.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Shall I disgrace my inheritance, Madam, by consulting my happiness?

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: Doubtless—if your happiness be consulted at the expense of your honour. Having been rejected by the versatile being whose affections you now boast of possessing, Miss Alford became your appointed bride. She, now in your castle, ready to obey the will of your mutual ancestor in becoming your wife, what honourable path remains for you, but as such to receive her?

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Madam, I can never—

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Still, I confess, the greatest delicacy ought to be observed towards her; and I am anxious for an explanation with her.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: And, during that explanation, my Lord, remember who you are—the representative of an illustrious house; who ought to consider, that, for the advantage of the titles and estates you derive from your ancestors, you owe some respect to what you may term their prejudices.

How strange his infatuation for this girl. What, if her partiality for Sir Harry be a falsehood? Was not my son the object of her contemptuous rejection? My Lord de Mallory, whence arises your degeneracy? She who bore you, never could forget an insult, nor ever missed the moment for revenging it. Ha! here comes one who may aid me most effectually.

Major Clayton, your presence here, which will be at all times highly gratifying, is now peculiarly desirable. I know your influence with my son; and you will not, I am sure, abet him in acting contrary to his honour.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: You may be assured of that, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: His marriage with Miss Alford, which must immediately take place—

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Would indeed be contrary to his honour.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: Sir, I wish strongly to recommend it.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: I am sorry for it, Madam, for I cannot.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: You would not, surely, recommend his marriage with Lady Julia, whose conduct I cannot reflect on but with indignation.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: I thought we were on the subject of your son's honour, not of your Ladyship's resentment.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: Can they be separated?

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: In this instance, I am certain they never can be united.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: I see your friendship prompts you to accord with my son's inclinations: I cannot but feel surprised at this, when I consider the liberty Lord de Mallory took with your name.

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: For which liberty with my name, all I require, is, Madam, that he may leave no blemish on it.—But 'tis impossible he should—He is a British Peer, and I a British Soldier—Honour is the bond of both. Lord de Mallory, be assured, will fulfil every engagement to which he has pledged the name of Clayton.Your Ladyship may now perceive that my honour is committed with your son's, for the completion of his union with Lady Julia Sandford—Of course, it must be as impossible for you to require me, as for me to consent to become the instrument of my own disgrace.

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.p: The time approaches rapidly for the completion of the prescribed marriage with one of my relatives, or the forfeiture of my fortune. Welcome ruin, in preference to an union but with my adored Julia. Her brother must long since have reached the Lake of Windermere—have removed his sister's prepossessions and explained that the supposed Clayton, who apparently rejected her, will sooner perish than accept the hand of another—Here is Miss Alford—My task, now, is a very perplexing one— to tell a pretty young woman, that it is impossible for me to love her.
Miss Alford, I have solicited this interview to pour out my whole heart to you.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: His whole heart—oh, he loves me, and I am undone.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: To talk of tender sentiments and the force of inclination would be deemed by many of our rank as a vulgar deviation from the cold system of noble alliance.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Oh, I am in a pitiable situation!

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: She seems much agitated—I fear her wishes strongly incline her to this union, and I hardly know how to proceed—but I must be explicit.
Madam, I have to declare to you, that a passion of the most fervent nature—

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: My Lord—Since I must speak, I had better get it over.—
Though my delicacy is wounded at what I am to utter, yet I must express to your Lordship, the state of my heart—it is so absolutely devoted—

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Dear Madam, how much you honour me beyond my merit!—Here's a predicament!

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: My Lord—I was going to say—

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: I feel all, Madam, that you were going to say.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: No, indeed, my Lord, you do not.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Don't let your delicacy be further wounded, by saying a syllable more.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Oh yes, my Lord—my delicacy will be shockingly wounded, unless I say a great deal more; for—for I believe your Lordship has a little misunderstood me—I was going to say, that— that my heart is so absolutely devoted to another.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: To another, Madam!

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Now, don't be so violent—yes, my Lord, to another,—and therefore, the passion your Lordship was so good as to express for me—

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: My dear Miss Alford—

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Now don't frighten me.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: This is really so strange.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Lord! he is quite hysterical with passion—I'll get away from him.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Stay till I explain.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Well, I will, if you will be calm.—

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: I am too happy to be very calm— for I was going to declare to you, that my heart is absolutely devoted to another.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Now, were you, upon your honour?

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: I was, indeed.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: And you really don't care at all, for me?

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Not a—Oh! yes, very much,— as my cousin.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Your indifference is charming—my dear, dear Lord, I can kiss you as my cousin; which I assure you I never could have done, as my husband. Now, for Heaven's sake, let us keep our real sentiments concealed from Lady de Mallory as long as we can—I so dread her anger. Let her believe we are quite charmed with each other.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Certainly—any thing you desire.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: But how shall we contrive at last to avoid the noose they are preparing for us?

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Are you determined to refuse me, at all events?

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Oh, most absolutely.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Then the worst that can happen, is a sacrifice of fortune.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: It can scarcely be considered a sacrifice when we part with fortune to maintain the freedom of the heart.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: I congratulate you, my dear cousin, on possessing the wisdom which the insensible call romance—to determine on the enjoyment of happiness, under any privation, with the man of your choice, rather than make a cold compromise for gloomy splendour, and heartless society, at the expense of the only true delight of life—domestic bliss.

div.stage: Scene continues—Lady Julia enters, conducted by Randall.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: My brother, you say, has quitted the Castle—then, wherefore should you urge me to remain? I came to vindicate myself to him— To no one else do I owe an explanation of my conduct.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Yes, my dear Lady—you owe it to yourself. ‘Do not let your pride aid the malice of your enemies.’

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: ‘Still, I will not avow myself until my brother's return, therefore, I must desire you for the present to obtain for me, a secure retreat.’

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: And will you leave the Castle, without seeing Lord de Mallory?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: No longer press me to behold the object of my aversion.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Will you refuse to gratify the fond wish— Call it a foolish one, if you please—of an old man who feels a Father's love for you?—Ha! I see my Lord, yonder.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Let me fly him.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Nay—he is not coming this way—See—he passes on.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: What! that—that, he? That, Lord de Mallory? Oh, Heaven!

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Lady Julia, you alarm me!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Don't be frightened—I am better— Oh, yes—much—much better—But are you certain—quite certain, that was Lord de Mallory?

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: How can you doubt it?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Indeed, indeed, I don't wish to doubt it—but I am so astonished—I should like to see him again—
but without being known to him. Tell me, where can you conceal me, that I may see him, undiscovered.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.stage: [pointing to a large stand of plants and flowers.]
sp.p: Place yourself there—Should he, or any one, come too near, you can make your retreat into my apartment. See, he is approaching.

div.stage: [They retire—She behind the flower-stand, he, into a Room near it.
Lord de Mallory enters, with a miniature picture in his hand.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Dear image of the beloved of my heart, but for thy solace, how insufferable were each moment unblest with her presence! With what redoubled delight I gaze upon thy charms, since the avowal which facilitates my union with thy adored original!—Here she comes whose charming ingenuousness has made me thus happy.

div.stage: [Lord de Mallory is near a Table, on which he lays the Picture, when he sees Miss Alford coming, and goes to meet her.

sp.speaker: Miss A.
sp.p: How differently we meet, now our hearts are open to each other—our brows are no longer clouded with distrust. Your mother is quite delighted at the change we exhibit—she wants to see you; and I undertook to bring you to her.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Thank you, my dear cousin.

sp.speaker: Miss A.
sp.p: No wonder she is pleased, when she finds me positively courting opportunities to be running after you—Aren't you highly flattered?

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Doubtless, after your frank declaration to me.

sp.speaker: Miss A.
sp.p: Well—no two beings ever avowed their sentiments more decidedly; and, I am sure, we can never doubt each other's sincerity.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: And may we, through life, be as happy as such sincerity deserves! If it were more generally practised, how much fewer would be the number of miserable alliances!

div.stage: [Exeunt Lord de M. and Miss Alford.
(Lady Julia comes forward in great agitation.)

sp.speaker: Lady Julia.
sp.p: Is there, on this earth, so wretched a being as myself?—'Tis all plain.—Resentment for my infatuated rejection of him, determined Lord De Mallory to feign a passion for me, for the purpose of rending my heart. He has succeeded— he is amply revenged!—Foolish, proud, weak girl, how have you trifled with your bliss! All is lost!— My cousin Harriet has his love—will be his wife— and I—Oh! I shall go distracted—
He has left her picture—with what rapture did he gaze on it! with what ecstasy did he kiss it,
sp.stage: (opening the case gradually, then looking with astonishment)
sp.p: Heaven! have I my senses?—it is— Oh, no—it can't be—Yes, it is—it is my—my picture.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Lady Julia—dear Lady Julia—‘this agitation—’

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: ‘Don't be alarmed—tell me—whose —whose likeness is this?’

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: ‘Yours, my sweet lady.’

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: ‘Are you sure? Indeed, I thought so; but still I feared I might be mistaken.’

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Now, let me hope you no longer wish to be concealed—let me tell Lord de Mallory—

sp.speaker: Lad. Jul.
sp.p: No, no, not yet—not yet: Lead me to your apartment—let Miss Alford only, know I am here; she can explain fully. Give me your arm—let us be gone—. I dread to meet Lady de Mallory. I feel at present quite unequal to such an encounter.—I am faint—very faint—but indeed, much, much happier.

So, here have I traced the impostor—the pretended Major Clayton. What tricks is he playing now, I wonder? Whom does he pass for in this castle?—One piece of good fortune results from this mishap,—it will be the means of introducing me to Lord de Mallory. His patronage may afford fine scope for the exertion of my talents. I wonder whether he has a borough vacant. Sir Harry Aspen!
Your most devoted servant. I have not had the pleasure of seeing you, Sir Harry, since that comical interview between you and the widow.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: It was very droll—very facetious, upon my honour—tho' you were a little angry at the moment, you must have had many a hearty laugh at it, since.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: Damnation!

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: To see the old Tabby with her arms so lovingly round your neck! I am sure you are a man that likes a joke, and therefore I must tell you that I have taken a sketch of the situation.—How you will laugh when you see it!

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.stage: (seizes him by the collar, frantic with rage.)

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: What the devil is the matter now.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: Mark me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: I don't mind death, Sir—

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: But I do; and to throttling, I have a peculiar aversion.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: Will you hear me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: With great pleasure, if you'll not let your action be quite so impressive.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: Then, Sir, if you don't tear your damned caricature into a thousand pieces, I'll tear you into as many—for I'd sooner be gibbeted for a murderer, on Hounslow Heath, than hung up for a fool in St. James's Street.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Oh—you don't like a joke—say no more, my dear Sir Harry; I'll never trouble you with one, either orally, in manuscript, in print, or etching.—Pray do me the honour to acknowledge me in this mansion—may be, you'll condescend so far as to present me—

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: Not I, Sir, don't cling to me for support. You are here on your own footing, and must make your own way.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Don't be so unforgiving—pardon me this once, Sir Harry—and now I find your nerves are so irritable, depend on it, I will never apply a stimulus to you again; I'll be as sheathing as oil, and as tranquillizing as opium.

div.head: SCENE the last.
div.stage: A grand Apartment in the Castle.
Lady DE Mallory enters, with Miss Alford in a Bridal Dress.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: Now for the completion of my wishes. My dear Harriet, with what delight I behold you arrayed as the bride of my son.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: I am happy to see your Ladyship. I hope I am not too late to have the pleasure of witnessing Lord De Mallory's nuptials.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: You are arrived in time, Sir Harry; let me present you to the bride—
and I hope my son will soon repay the compliment with which you honour him by witnessing (if it have not already taken place) your union with Lady Julia.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: My union with Lady Julia, Madam? I declare I—I don't know—I should be too happy— I—I am mortally afraid she is bantering me.

sp.speaker: Lady De M.
sp.p: You seem a little abashed, Sir Harry. Come, come; when Lord de Mallory is this lady's husband, you will feel less restraint in avowing your passion for her to whom he once was to have been allied.

sp.speaker: Doct. Suitall
sp.p: Now, do pray, let me see his lordship; my business is of the utmost consequence.

div.stage: Doctor Suitall enters, and a Servant.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: My lady, this gentleman will see his lordship, spite of all we can do to hinder him.

sp.speaker: Miss A.
sp.p: Permit me, Madam, to withdraw for a few moments.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: I beg your ladyship ten thousand pardons.—

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: You have chosen a strange time, Sir, for your intrusion. What is your business?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: To detect an impostor, Madam, whom I have traced to this noble mansion.—Ah ha! here he comes.

Have I found you, Sir? This is the fellow, Madam; I will rid the castle of him, I warrant you. Have you no more respect for the illustrious inhabitants of this stately pile than to intrude yourself here? Come, come, Sir, turn out, directly, before I expose your Windermere tricks.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: A lunatic!

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: No, no, madam—a sharper.
Major Clayton! this is luck, indeed. Here is the impostor who passed for you. Pray, who does he pass for here?

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: For Lord de Mallory.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: What! in Lord de Mallory's own castle?

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Yes: and here it would be impossible for him to pass for any body else.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Hey! why?

sp.speaker: Cl.
sp.p: Because he happens to be, really and truly, Lord de Mallory.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Oh dear!

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: Lord de Mallory! oh the devil! Then Lord de Mallory witnessed my scene with the widow.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Yes, Doctor, I am Lord de Mallory; and have certainly some excuses to make to you, for presenting myself in a feigned character.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Excuses, my dear Lord! You have honoured me beyond expression.—Peers, my Lord, have privileges—

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Yes, Doctor; but if joking be one, they don't often exercise it.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Here is a connection! I am a made man.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: My Lord, your bride approaches.

div.stage: [Lady Julia enters with bride-maids at the same door through which Miss Alford retired, dressed exactly like her—with a veil over her face.]

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: No intelligence from Julia yet!— her brother not returned! This dilemma is dreadful.

div.stage: [Lord de Mallory takes Lady Julia by the hand, and leads her forward.]

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.stage: [to Lady de M. and Sir Harry Aspen.]
sp.p: You are in expectation of an event which can never take place. I am prepared to make the sacrifice of my fortune, rather than unite myself in opposition to my inclinations! 'Tis a great alleviation to the distress of this moment, to know that the sentiments of the lady destined to be a joint victim, accord with my own.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: My Lord, you astonish me. Do not, in palliation of your headstrong conduct, attempt to misrepresent the sentiments of another. The Lady is disposed to obey the will of her ancestor, by receiving you as her husband.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: That shall soon be put to trial. Madam, are you not prepared to reject me?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: What! will you receive me as your husband?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Well, Madam! I shall not imitate your mutability. I reject you.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: No, no—don't say so.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: Julia!

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: To this dear girl I owe my happiness.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: I am filled with wonder and delight.

sp.speaker: Miss Al.
sp.p: Come, Madam,
do not suffer your regret to cloud our joy. It was vain to oppose destiny. My heart is devoted as irrevocably to the amiable brother of my friend, as hers to your son.

sp.speaker: Lady de M.
sp.p: Well—I will endeavour to extract happiness for myself from the general felicity.
She is here—Lady Julia is here, you say?

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Ha! have I found you at last?

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Yes; and you are just come in time to give me away to one, who, though he refused me as Major Clayton, is ready to receive me, as Lord de Mallory.

sp.speaker: Lord de M.
sp.p: And be assured, Sir, that Lord de Mallory is fully sensible of the blessing which awaits him.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: If you are happy I have my desire.

sp.speaker: Lady Julia.
sp.p: And here is one who partakes no small portion of the joy he has been so zealous to promote.

sp.speaker: Ran.
sp.p: Indeed, indeed, my heart is full of it.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: Disappointed in all my hopes, I had better quietly retire to hide my chagrin, and escape the horrors of ridicule.

div.stage: [As he is going Mrs. Leech enters.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: Sir Harry!

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: There, Sir Harry!—Reward her perseverance—Consider the journey she has taken in pursuit of you—and travelling at her time of life is a serious thing.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: This is all I wanted to make me completely frantic. In a few minutes I have lost the chance of a brilliant estate—of a lady I have long adored—and, to wind up all, I am to be laughed at by the world as this old mouser's Corydon.

sp.speaker: Mrs. L.
sp.p: What! deserted and insulted? Here is treatment! But I will expose your perfidy, and give a fresh warning to sensitive hearts, not to trust perfidious man—I will be revenged, you barbarous monster!

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Sir Harry don't be agitated—she has connections, and you have patronage—if you'll sweeten the dose I am ready to swallow it for your sake; and will draw off her vengeance from you, by marrying her myself.

sp.speaker: Sir Har.
sp.p: Will you be such a friend?

sp.speaker: Lady Julia.
sp.stage: (coming forward with Ellen, Lord de Mallory, Major Clayton, &c. who have been talking apart.)
sp.p: And my dear Ellen's marriage shall be celebrated with mine. My own happiness, my sweet girl, is augmented by yours.

sp.speaker: Ellen.
sp.p: You are too kind—indeed I am happy far beyond my humble merit.

sp.speaker: Lady Jul.
sp.p: Not so; for sweetness of temper and innocence like your's can never be rewarded too highly.—While you prove that native virtues in humble life, may lead to an elevated station, I was very near exhibiting a fatal instance of precipitate decision, in rejecting him whom I now feel I was born to love.

sp.speaker: Heart.
sp.p: Well, well, all is right at last, and I shall resume my old partiality—in which I hope I am not singular—for it is my hearty wish, that every one here may look with satisfaction at the Gazette Extraordinary.
